lessons.title: Life, as it could be
lessons.subtitle: The big questions behind artificial life

sections.title: A different lens
sections.text: ALIFE studies the processes that make life possible, including forms that do not occur on Earth. AI focuses on intelligent behaviour; the fields overlap in adaptive agents and learning. A useful test: are you studying life processes, intelligent performance, or both?

sections.title: Three laboratories
sections.text: Soft ALIFE uses digital systems, hard ALIFE uses physical robots, and wet ALIFE uses biochemical systems. Strong ALIFE claims an artificial system can literally be alive; weak ALIFE uses models to understand living processes. A successful simulation alone does not settle this philosophical distinction.

sections.title: An ecology inside a computer
sections.text: In Tierra, self-replicating programs compete for memory and execution time. Parasites exploit host replication machinery. Adaptation changes the ecological opportunities of other programs: connect this to co-evolution in Lecture 9.

sections.title: Open-ended is a demanding claim
sections.text: A long simulation is not sufficient evidence of open-ended evolution. Ask whether heritable variation and selection keep producing new forms and new ecological possibilities, rather than merely repeating behaviours.

lessons.recall: Can something resemble an animal without reproducing or evolving? Explain which ALIFE claim you would be comfortable making.

lessons.title: Small rules. Complex worlds.
lessons.subtitle: Cellular automata and Conway’s Game of Life

sections.title: Local information, global patterns
sections.text: A cellular automaton has a lattice, discrete cell states, a neighbourhood and an update rule. Game of Life uses eight surrounding cells: the Moore neighbourhood. Update all cells simultaneously from the previous generation.

sections.title: B3 / S23
sections.text: A dead cell is born with exactly three live neighbours. A live cell survives with two or three. All other cells are dead in the next generation. Try predicting a blinker before pressing Step in the lab.

sections.title: Persistence is not all the same
sections.text: A block is a still life, a blinker an oscillator, and a glider translates across the lattice. Pattern names describe outcomes of local rules; cells do not know the global pattern.

sections.title: Replication needs interpretation
sections.text: Crystal growth and prion propagation illustrate replication of patterns. They are not automatically equivalent to a general constructor reproducing its inherited organisation. Separate a demonstrated mechanism from a claim about life.

lessons.recall: Why would updating cells one at a time in place change the model?

lessons.title: Behaviour without a blueprint
lessons.subtitle: Agents, Braitenberg vehicles and emergence

sections.title: Sense → act, or sense → plan → act?
sections.text: Reactive agents map current sensory input to actions. Deliberative agents maintain a world model and plan. A complex-looking trajectory alone does not establish deliberation, cognition or learning.

sections.title: Braitenberg’s thought experiment
sections.text: Simple sensor-to-motor wiring can produce behaviour observers describe as fear, aggression, love or exploration. Excitatory versus inhibitory connections and crossed versus uncrossed wiring change turning behaviour. Explain the circuit before assigning an emotion.

sections.title: Function and interpretation
sections.text: A functional description specifies how sensor values determine motors. An ethological description names the observed behaviour. Braitenberg vehicles expose how easily observers infer complex internal causes from simple functional mechanisms.

sections.title: From individuals to collectives
sections.text: Biomimicry takes inspiration from biological forms or processes. Emergence describes macro patterns arising from component interactions. Neither appearance alone nor a complicated animation proves life, intelligence or open-ended evolution.

lessons.recall: If two sensors return the same value, will symmetric motor wiring produce a turn? What breaks the symmetry?

lessons.title: The collective takes shape
lessons.subtitle: Boids, stigmergy and agent-based models

sections.title: Build the mechanism first
sections.text: An ABM specifies agents, states, an environment and interaction rules. Its value comes from testing whether local mechanisms generate a collective pattern, not merely making a convincing animation.

sections.title: Three steering tendencies
sections.text: Separation steers away from close neighbours. Alignment steers toward local average heading or velocity. Cohesion steers toward local average position. The balance of these tendencies gives flocking; change weights and radii to test the result.

sections.title: Stigmergy: leave a trace
sections.text: Agents can coordinate through a shared environmental structure. A construction or pheromone trace changes what subsequent agents sense and do. This connects nest construction with distributed coordination without a blueprint.

sections.title: The cybernetic wasteland
sections.text: The lecturer’s cybernetic wasteland concern is specific: societal ABMs can contain pre-programmed rational agents that react to environmental pressures but lack psychological, emotional and personality traits. This can omit mechanisms behind human decisions. Compare explicit behavioural hypotheses and validate them against evidence; historical psychological states are particularly hard to establish.

lessons.recall: If cohesion is high and separation is zero, what pattern do you predict? Test it in the Boids lab.

lessons.title: How a neighbourhood tips
lessons.subtitle: Schelling’s model and phase transitions

sections.title: Local satisfaction
sections.text: An agent is happy when the proportion of occupied neighbours of the same group meets its threshold. Vacant cells do not enter that fraction. Specify what happens for an isolated agent; our lab treats it as satisfied.

sections.title: Tolerance can still yield clustering
sections.text: A preference for roughly one-third similar neighbours can produce substantial clustering under the illustrated settings. This is not a universal threshold: density, neighbourhood, group ratios and move rules matter.

sections.title: Run an experiment
sections.text: Begin mixed, measure satisfaction and clustering, then change one parameter. Repeat with fresh initial conditions. Outcomes depend on stochastic movement and finite boundaries; a single run is an observation, not a theorem.

sections.title: Useful and limited
sections.text: Schelling’s model isolates a mechanism for self-organisation. It omits many economic, institutional and historical forces. A tipping point in a model is a hypothesis-generating result, not a complete causal account of a city.

lessons.recall: Could every agent tolerate a majority of unlike neighbours while the city still clusters? Explain the feedback.

lessons.title: Evolution as a search engine
lessons.subtitle: Representations, fitness and the EA loop

sections.title: Encode, evaluate, vary
sections.text: An EA maintains a population of encoded solutions. Decode genotypes into testable phenotypes, evaluate fitness, select parents, create variation and choose survivors. Parent selection and survivor selection answer different questions.

sections.title: Representation shapes possibility
sections.text: Binary strings, real vectors, trees and graphs imply different search spaces and valid operators. Selection acts on evaluated phenotypic performance while inherited representations are varied. An unsuitable encoding can make useful solutions hard to reach.

sections.title: Guided stochastic search
sections.text: Mutation and recombination propose candidates. Selection biases which candidates contribute. Randomness is guided by evaluation; it does not guarantee monotonic improvement or a global optimum in a finite run.

sections.title: A landscape is a model
sections.text: A fitness landscape relates encoded configurations to fitness under a chosen neighbourhood. Ruggedness, multiple optima and variable interactions can make search difficult. In co-evolution the landscape itself changes as other populations adapt.

lessons.recall: Why can changing an encoding change which mutations are small?

lessons.title: Variation and survival
lessons.subtitle: Mutation, recombination and selection

sections.title: Mutation opens possibilities
sections.text: Mutation is unary: it modifies one parent. A bit-flip mutation changes each bit independently with probability pm in the standard bitwise version. For L bits the expected number of flips is Lpm; expectation is not an observed count.

sections.title: Crossover mixes inherited material
sections.text: One-point crossover cuts two compatible strings at the same position and exchanges suffixes. It can produce fitter or weaker children. It cannot invent an allele absent from both parents at the same locus.

sections.title: Two kinds of selection
sections.text: Parent selection chooses contributors to reproduction. Survivor selection decides who enters the next population. Full generational replacement can discard the best parent; elitism retains selected best individuals.

sections.title: Roulette is probabilistic
sections.text: For nonnegative fitness values with positive total, pi = fi / Σf. In m independent draws the expected count is mpi. The actual count is an integer and can differ greatly from its expectation.

lessons.recall: If a genotype has probability 0.4, is it guaranteed two copies in five draws?

lessons.title: A genetic algorithm, under the lens
lessons.subtitle: Worked arithmetic, landscapes and replacement

sections.title: Walk through the worked example
sections.text: For x² on integers 0…31, five bits encode x. The initial values 13, 24, 8 and 19 have fitness 169, 576, 64 and 361: total 1170 and mean 292.5. Expected roulette copies equal 4fi/1170; observed copies need not match.

sections.title: Read the arithmetic critically
sections.text: The shown mutated strings 11100, 11001, 11011 and 10010 decode to 28, 25, 27 and 18. Their fitness total is 2462 and mean 615.5. Lecture 8 notes discuss inconsistent per-genotype and per-bit mutation interpretations: explicitly state which model you calculate with.

sections.title: Replacement has a fraction
sections.text: Generation gap = number replaced / population size. Generational replacement gives 1; a small steady-state update gives a small fraction. Full replacement alone does not preserve the best candidate.

sections.title: Landscapes and mixing bias
sections.text: The standard sphere Σxj² is smooth, convex, separable, unimodal and well conditioned. Nonlinear does not imply rugged. One-point crossover depends on gene order; uniform crossover independently samples parental sources at each locus.

lessons.recall: For parents 0000 and 1111, can one-point crossover produce 0101? Can uniform crossover?

lessons.title: Who gets to reproduce?
lessons.subtitle: Ranking, tournament selection and co-evolution

sections.title: Rank instead of magnitude
sections.text: Rank 1 is worst and rank N best. Linear ranking uses p(i) = [n− +(n+ − n−)(i−1)/(N−1)]/N, with n− = 2−n+ and 1≤n+≤2. It depends on ordering rather than raw score differences.

sections.title: Tournament size is a pressure dial
sections.text: Sample k candidates and select the fittest. Increasing k favours high ranks, usually increasing selection intensity and loss of diversity. Sampling with or without replacement changes exact probabilities: state your convention.

sections.title: Three quantities, three definitions
sections.text: Selection intensity measures the increase of mean fitness after selection. Loss of diversity is the proportion of genotypes not selected per generation. Selection variance is the normalised variance of fitness after selection; it is not the variance in copy counts across trials.

sections.title: When the opponent changes the task
sections.text: Co-evolution couples fitness landscapes. Adaptation in one population changes what succeeds in the other. Competitive and cooperative co-evolution differ in how participants contribute to the evaluation; the Red Queen effect can hide change behind stable relative success.

lessons.recall: Why can fitness variance approach zero while the mean selected fitness increases?

lessons.title: Evolving bodies and opponents
lessons.subtitle: Sims’ creatures and robotic ALIFE

sections.title: A graph becomes a body
sections.text: Sims’ creature genotype is a variable-length directed graph describing body parts and associated control. Evolution can change morphology and controller together: representation determines what bodies can be constructed.

sections.title: Evaluation against another organism
sections.text: In competitive co-evolution, a candidate’s score depends on opponents. Changing opponents can reverse which candidate is best. Testing against a fixed archive can help distinguish progress from cycling or overspecialisation.

sections.title: Robot, android, organism?
sections.text: A robot is a physical machine capable of acting; an android has human form. Hard ALIFE uses robotic systems to investigate life-like organisation or behaviour. Human resemblance alone does not establish cognition or literal life.

sections.title: Cognition is task dependent
sections.text: Simple reactive or passive physical systems can generate life-like behaviour. Some interaction tasks require richer modelling of others. Start with the task and demonstrated mechanism rather than inferring cognition from appearance.

lessons.recall: What would you measure to distinguish a general improvement from merely beating the current opponent?

lessons.title: When machines feel almost human
lessons.subtitle: Morphological computation and the uncanny valley

sections.title: The body participates
sections.text: Morphological computation describes physical body properties doing work that would otherwise require explicit control computation. Compliance, shape and passive dynamics can simplify control. It is a useful mechanism, not a requirement for all life-like behaviour.

sections.title: An almost-human dip
sections.text: The uncanny valley hypothesis describes negative reactions to some nearly human agents. Do not assume everyone experiences it, or that human likeness has a single objective scale. Appearance, movement and context can interact.

sections.title: Separate competing explanations
sections.text: Anomaly recognition concerns features that violate expectations. Perceptual tension concerns conflicting cues, such as human appearance with unnatural movement. Vary appearance and motion independently to distinguish these hypotheses.

sections.title: Design for evidence
sections.text: Use comparison conditions, counterbalance presentation order and measure reported eeriness or affinity. Keep lighting, task and dialogue comparable. A convincing design predicts different outcomes under competing explanations.

lessons.recall: How would you isolate an unnatural facial feature from an unnatural motion pattern?

lessons.title: The uncanny, in the wild
lessons.subtitle: Bonus source: field studies and research limits

sections.title: Beyond a controlled laboratory
sections.text: The additional Lecture 12 deck describes unscripted encounters with an android in a café. Field context improves ecological relevance while reducing control over participants and prior expectations.

sections.title: What did the sample capture?
sections.text: Only participants agreeing to interviews entered the video evaluation. This may introduce selection bias. Unprompted comments and explicitly elicited feelings are different kinds of evidence.

sections.title: Connect back to the beginning
sections.text: Robotics experiments, ABMs and digital evolution all ask whether a mechanism explains an observation. Identify the research question, implementation medium, evidence and limitations before making claims about life or cognition.

lessons.recall: How might people who decline an interview differ from those who agree?

questions.explanation: Selection variance = (1/6)/(2/3) = 1/4. This is fitness variance after selection normalised by before-selection variance.
questions.hint: Selection variance = (1/6)/(2/3) = 1/4.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: N=6, n+=1.8, n−=0.2, rank 6 is best. What is its linear ranking selection probability?
questions.explanation: For the best rank, p = n+/N = 1.8/6 = 0.3.
questions.hint: For the best rank, p = n+/N = 1.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: With N=4 distinct ranks and k=2 independent draws with replacement, what is the winning probability of rank 2 (rank 1 worst)?
questions.hint: P(rank i wins) = (i/N)^k − ((i−1)/N)^k.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: Distinguish genetic drift from fitness-based selection and propose a mitigation.
questions.answer: Drift is random change in genotype or allele frequencies due to finite sampling; It can remove diversity even among equally fit candidates; Increase population size or use diversity preservation such as niching; Explain how the intervention reduces accidental loss or maintains alternatives
questions.explanation: Drift is not the same as systematic preference for higher fitness. Mitigation is not a guarantee of elimination.
questions.hint: Drift is not the same as systematic preference for higher fitness.
rubric: Drift is random change in genotype or allele frequencies due to finite sampling
It can remove diversity even among equally fit candidates
Increase population size or use diversity preservation such as niching
Explain how the intervention reduces accidental loss or maintains alternatives
questions.mistakes: Do not define drift as systematic selection of fitter candidates. Random sampling can change frequencies even when all fitnesses are equal.

questions.text: In competitive co-evolution the fitness landscape is necessarily fixed.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: An opponent’s adaptation changes the evaluation context and hence the effective landscape.
questions.hint: An opponent’s adaptation changes the evaluation context and hence the effective landscape.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: Distinguish a robot from an android and explain when either could support hard ALIFE research.
questions.answer: A robot is a physical acting machine; An android has human form; Either can investigate life-like processes or behaviour; Appearance alone does not prove life or cognition
questions.explanation: Connect the research purpose to ALIFE rather than classifying every machine as alive.
questions.hint: Connect the research purpose to ALIFE rather than classifying every machine as alive.
rubric: A robot is a physical acting machine
An android has human form
Either can investigate life-like processes or behaviour
Appearance alone does not prove life or cognition
questions.mistakes: Do not treat every robot as an android, or human shape as proof of life or cognition. Explain the life-process research purpose.

questions.text: What makes Sims’ representation especially relevant to body–controller co-design?
questions.answer: A graph encodes body structure and associated control
questions.explanation: Variation can change both morphology and the neural control structure.
options: A graph encodes body structure and associated control
Every creature has a fixed human body
Fitness never depends on an opponent
questions.hint: Variation can change both morphology and the neural control structure.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: Explain the Red Queen effect and give a useful evaluation precaution.
questions.answer: Opponents continually co-adapt; Relative success can remain unchanged despite adaptation; Evaluate against archived or standard opponents as well as current ones
questions.explanation: A flat relative score does not necessarily indicate an absence of evolution.
questions.hint: A flat relative score does not necessarily indicate an absence of evolution.
rubric: Opponents continually co-adapt
Relative success can remain unchanged despite adaptation
Evaluate against archived or standard opponents as well as current ones
questions.mistakes: Do not assume fitness is an absolute, unchanging score. A current win can reflect opponent specialisation rather than general improvement.

questions.text: Explain how body mechanics can simplify robotic control and why this does not make cognition necessary for all life-like behaviour.
questions.answer: Physical properties can stabilise or coordinate movement; This reduces explicit controller computation; Reactive or passive mechanisms can create life-like movement without deliberation
questions.explanation: A mechanism is not a universal prerequisite.
questions.hint: A mechanism is not a universal prerequisite.
rubric: Physical properties can stabilise or coordinate movement
This reduces explicit controller computation
Reactive or passive mechanisms can create life-like movement without deliberation
questions.mistakes: Do not equate physical simplification of control with conscious reasoning, or claim morphological computation is necessary for every lifelike robot.

questions.text: Design an experiment that separates anomaly recognition from appearance–motion conflict as explanations for uncanny responses.
questions.answer: Manipulate anomalous versus consistent facial features; Independently manipulate natural versus unnatural motion; Compare conditions with otherwise matched stimuli; Measure eeriness or affinity and counterbalance order; Predict a feature effect for anomalies versus a mismatch effect for conflicting cues
questions.explanation: Original mock-inspired design: credit manipulations, controls, measurement and distinguishable predictions. It is not a lecturer-supplied marking memo.
questions.hint: Original mock-inspired design: credit manipulations, controls, measurement and distinguishable predictions.
rubric: Manipulate anomalous versus consistent facial features
Independently manipulate natural versus unnatural motion
Compare conditions with otherwise matched stimuli
Measure eeriness or affinity and counterbalance order
Predict a feature effect for anomalies versus a mismatch effect for conflicting cues
questions.mistakes: Do not manipulate appearance and movement together without comparison conditions. A single disliked android does not establish a valley; specify measures, controls and competing predictions.

questions.text: Which condition most directly tests perceptual tension?
questions.answer: Human-like appearance paired with mechanical motion
questions.explanation: The hypothesis concerns conflicting perceptual cues.
options: Human-like appearance paired with mechanical motion
questions.hint: The hypothesis concerns conflicting perceptual cues.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: Every life-like robot must use morphological computation.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Morphology can simplify control, but life-like behaviour can also be produced by other mechanisms.
questions.hint: Morphology can simplify control, but life-like behaviour can also be produced by other mechanisms.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: Explain a limitation of evaluating only people who agree to interviews in an android field study.
questions.answer: Agreement may correlate with attitudes or comfort around robots; The analysed sample can therefore be systematically unrepresentative; Report recruitment and compare inclusion patterns where possible
questions.explanation: This is selection bias, not merely a small sample.
questions.hint: This is selection bias, not merely a small sample.
rubric: Agreement may correlate with attitudes or comfort around robots
The analysed sample can therefore be systematically unrepresentative
Report recruitment and compare inclusion patterns where possible
questions.mistakes: Do not assume interview volunteers represent all passers-by. Distinguish selection bias from random sampling uncertainty and ecological validity from experimental control.

questions.text: An unscripted field encounter gives the same experimental control as a randomised laboratory study.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Real-world context increases ecological relevance but introduces uncontrolled differences.
questions.hint: Real-world context increases ecological relevance but introduces uncontrolled differences.
questions.mistakes: Distinguish the mechanism from the observed result. State assumptions and justify each claim.

questions.text: Why can a Tierra parasite gain a short-term advantage without an all-parasite population being viable?
questions.answer: It exploits replication machinery supplied by hosts; Avoiding its own machinery can reduce its reproductive cost; Without suitable hosts its replication opportunity disappears
questions.explanation: The ecology makes fitness context dependent; individual reproductive advantage does not imply population viability.
questions.hint: Identify the mechanism and distinguish it from the observed outcome.
rubric: It exploits replication machinery supplied by hosts
Avoiding its own machinery can reduce its reproductive cost
Without suitable hosts its replication opportunity disappears
questions.mistakes: Runtime alone does not establish open-ended evolution. For parasites, distinguish individual advantage from dependence on host resources.

questions.text: Two symmetric light sensors give equal readings. What do symmetric motor connections predict, and how could a controller escape a head-on situation?
questions.answer: Equal symmetric inputs produce equal motor commands; There is no turning bias; Add asymmetry noise memory or an explicit avoidance rule
questions.explanation: This is a boundary case of the sense–act mapping, not evidence of intention.
questions.hint: Identify the mechanism and distinguish it from the observed outcome.
rubric: Equal symmetric inputs produce equal motor commands
There is no turning bias
Add asymmetry noise memory or an explicit avoidance rule
questions.mistakes: Do not infer emotions or deliberation from observer descriptions. Specify the sensor–motor mapping and address symmetry when input readings are equal.

questions.text: Why might a society model of entirely utility-maximising agents become a cybernetic wasteland, and could a similar concern apply to android research?
questions.answer: It can omit emotion psychology personality and social motivations; Plausible collective patterns need not explain human decisions; An android can likewise appear human while lacking the mechanisms being attributed to it; Relevance depends on the research question and required explanatory fidelity
questions.explanation: The extension to androids is original mock-inspired reasoning, not a claim that every robot needs human psychology.
questions.hint: Identify the mechanism and distinguish it from the observed outcome.
rubric: It can omit emotion psychology personality and social motivations
Plausible collective patterns need not explain human decisions
An android can likewise appear human while lacking the mechanisms being attributed to it
Relevance depends on the research question and required explanatory fidelity
questions.mistakes: Do not use this merely as a synonym for a boring model. The course critique specifically concerns agents lacking personality, emotion and psychology.

questions.text: Does a stable Schelling configuration necessarily imply strong segregation? Explain what you would measure.
questions.answer: Stability means no agent needs or makes a move under the rule; Segregation concerns spatial clustering by group; Measure local similarity or clustering as well as satisfaction and movement
questions.explanation: A mixed configuration can be stable at low preferences. Separate dynamical and spatial outcomes.
questions.hint: Identify the mechanism and distinguish it from the observed outcome.
rubric: Stability means no agent needs or makes a move under the rule
Segregation concerns spatial clustering by group
Measure local similarity or clustering as well as satisfaction and movement
questions.mistakes: Do not count empty cells as other-group agents. High satisfaction is not the same measurement as clustering, and the illustrative one-third threshold is not universal.

questions.text: In what sense is an EA an anytime algorithm, and what additional mechanism preserves the best result found?
questions.answer: It can report its best available candidate when interrupted; More computation provides further search opportunities without guaranteeing a better candidate each generation; An external best-so-far archive or elitism retains the best discovered result
questions.explanation: Distinguish best current population member from best ever evaluated candidate.
questions.hint: Identify the mechanism and distinguish it from the observed outcome.
rubric: It can report its best available candidate when interrupted
More computation provides further search opportunities without guaranteeing a better candidate each generation
An external best-so-far archive or elitism retains the best discovered result
questions.mistakes: Do not promise a finite-time global optimum. Separate a nonzero chance of reaching an optimum from retaining it, and separate best current from best-ever fitness.

questions.text: Why is nonlinear an insufficient reason to call a function rugged or a good target for an EA? Use the sphere as a counterexample.
questions.answer: The sphere is nonlinear but smooth convex and quadratic; Its variables are separable and its optimum is at the origin; Specialised methods can exploit this structure more efficiently; Choose an EA based on problem properties rather than a nonlinear label
questions.explanation: This converts the sphere slide’s checklist into a reasoning question; no general EA superiority is claimed.
questions.hint: Identify the mechanism and distinguish it from the observed outcome.
rubric: The sphere is nonlinear but smooth convex and quadratic
Its variables are separable and its optimum is at the origin
Specialised methods can exploit this structure more efficiently
Choose an EA based on problem properties rather than a nonlinear label
questions.mistakes: Do not label every nonlinear function rugged or non-convex. The standard sphere is nonlinear, smooth, quadratic, separable and unimodal.
